issues.legal_issue: An acquittal in a group-violence murder case may be set aside for accused whose participation and shared unlawful object are established by reliable evidence, while retained for those not sufficiently linked to the crimes.
material_facts: Three people were killed during a group assault involving multiple assailants and different weapons.
Three eyewitnesses described the assault; two were searching for a missing animal, and the third was a young relative of the victims who had brought them food.
The High Court rejected the eyewitness accounts based on the witnesses’ presence, relationship to the victims, an alleged medical discrepancy, delay in reporting, and lack of proven motive.

The Supreme Court found those criticisms insufficient to discredit the witnesses’ accounts, but found reasonable doubt as to some accused because two were not named in the initial report and the evidence did not establish that two others shared the object of committing murder.
issues.conclusion: The acquittals were set aside and convictions for rioting and murder with a shared unlawful object were entered for the five accused whose participation was established. The acquittals of four others on those charges were upheld.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court ordinarily does not interfere with an acquittal, but may do so when the court below overlooked important facts and relied on circumstances that did not impair the probative value of the evidence. A chance witness is not necessarily incredible, though the evidence requires cautious and close scrutiny; relationship alone does not make a witness suspect; discrepancies about which assailant used which weapon are not necessarily fatal in a group assault; and where reliable eyewitness, medical, and prompt-report evidence proves the crimes, motive need not be established. The Court applied Sections 148 and 302 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code. It referred generally to this Court’s repeated statements about related witnesses but named no earlier case.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and high_court_overlooked_material_evidence and credible_eyewitness_accounts and corroborating_evidence and (individual_participation_proved and shared_unlawful_object_proved)

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution or an affected person appealed against an acquittal in a criminal case.
predicates.high_court_overlooked_material_evidence: The appellate court below overlooked important evidence or relied on circumstances that did not undermine the evidence’s probative value.
predicates.credible_eyewitness_accounts: Eyewitnesses gave accounts of the incident that remained credible after scrutiny, notwithstanding their chance presence or relationship to victims.
predicates.corroborating_evidence: Other evidence, including medical or prompt-report evidence, supported the eyewitness accounts.
predicates.individual_participation_proved: The evidence sufficiently identified an accused as participating in the assault.
predicates.shared_unlawful_object_proved: The evidence established that an accused shared the group’s unlawful object to commit the crimes.

issues.definition: When an acquittal appeal involves overlooked material evidence and credible, corroborated eyewitness accounts, the acquittal is reversed for accused whose participation and shared unlawful object are proved, but retained for those not sufficiently linked.

issues.legal_issue: An acquittal on a conspiracy charge should stand when the evidence offered to prove the alleged agreement is unreliable.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged that three accused had discussed exterminating one of the victims before the killings.
The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court that the evidence offered to prove that discussion and conspiracy did not inspire confidence.
issues.conclusion: The acquittals on the criminal-conspiracy charge were upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The Court found the prosecution evidence of conspiracy unreliable and upheld the acquittal under Section 120B of the Indian Penal Code. The judgment identifies no earlier case or more specific legal test for this conclusion.

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The prosecution or an affected person appealed against an acquittal in a criminal case.
predicates.conspiracy_alleged: The prosecution alleged that the accused had agreed to commit a crime.
predicates.evidence_of_agreement_unreliable: The evidence offered to establish the alleged agreement did not inspire confidence.

issues.definition: When an acquittal appeal concerns an alleged criminal agreement and the evidence of that agreement is unreliable, the acquittal on the conspiracy charge stands.

issues.legal_issue: A death sentence need not be restored when substantial time has elapsed before the final appellate decision.
material_facts: The trial court had imposed death sentences on three accused convicted of murder committed as part of a group assault.
More than ten years had elapsed since the offences when the Supreme Court considered whether to restore those sentences.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to restore the death sentences and imposed life imprisonment for the murder convictions.
issues.legal_principle: In considering the sentence after restoring the murder convictions, the Court treated the lapse of more than ten years since the offences as a reason not to restore the death sentences. It imposed life imprisonment for the convictions under Section 302 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code.

predicates.appellate_review_of_death_sentence: An appellate court considered whether to restore a death sentence imposed for a murder conviction.
predicates.substantial_lapse_before_final_decision: A substantial period elapsed between the offence and the final appellate decision on sentence.

issues.definition: When an appellate court reviews a death sentence after a substantial lapse before the final decision, it may decline to restore the death sentence and impose life imprisonment.
